standard_text: Apply the properties of operations (i.e., identity, inverse, commutative, associative, distributive properties) to create equivalent linear expressions and to justify whether two linear expressions are equivalent when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them. (E)

progression.narrative: 6.NS.7 asks students to create equivalent linear expressions using the properties of operations and to justify equivalence by substituting a value into both expressions. The on-grade work builds in order: name the parts of an expression, combine like terms, rearrange with the commutative and associative properties, distribute a factor across a sum, and then prove equivalence by testing values. Students who stall here are usually missing arithmetic from below grade six, most often shaky multiplication facts that make distributing and factoring slow and error prone. The grade five gaps that block this work most are weak order of operations and never having written or read an expression such as three times a sum. Intervention should rebuild the facts and the number based distributive property first, then the grade five expression skills, and only then return to variables.

steps.rationale: Name the parts. Every property is a statement about what may move or merge, so students must first see 5x + 8 as a coefficient, a variable, and a constant -- separate terms, not one blob of symbols.
The first way to create an equivalent expression: merge like terms. 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r and 9r + 8 name the same number, and only terms that count the same thing can be combined.

The commutative and associative properties are the license behind rearranging and regrouping -- and they only cover addition and multiplication. Knowing where the license STOPS (subtraction, division) is half the skill.

The distributive property is the standard's central transformation: 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15, in both directions (expanding and factoring with the GCF). The multiplier must reach both terms in the parentheses.

The standard's own definition of equivalent: the two expressions name the same number for EVERY value substituted in. Substitution turns 'are these equivalent?' from a guess about appearance into a checkable fact.
The full demand: chain the properties together -- distribute, rearrange, combine like terms -- to simplify multi-step expressions and to write several different equivalent forms of one expression.

skills.name: Recall multiplication and division facts

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply and divide fluently within 100, including the related division facts.

skills.i_do_script: 7 x 6 is a picture before it is a fact: 7 rows with 6 dots in each row. Adding the two numbers gives only 13, not even two full rows, which is why multiplying and adding land so far apart. We are warming up the facts you lean on all through this standard. To expand 4(3x + 5) you need 4 x 3 and 4 x 5 the instant you see them, and to factor 12x + 8 you need to notice that 4 divides both 12 and 8. Watch: 4 x 3 is 12 and 4 x 5 is 20, known, not counted, and that instant knowing is what we build today.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the factors instead of multiplying, or skip counts and stops one row short
canonical_error.example: For 7 x 6, answers 13 (added 7 and 6) or 35 (counted only five rows of 7)
canonical_error.why: The fact is not automatic yet, so the student falls back on a slower strategy and slips under time pressure, adding because it is easier or losing count partway through skip counting.

skills.item_template: A single multiplication or division fact within 100, answered from memory. NR response, no choices. Short stems for a timed fluency sprint.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 13 (added the factors); 35 (a row short)
12 (added); 24 (used 8 x 3)
15 (added); 45 (used 9 x 5)
15 (added); 33 (a group short)
15 (added); 48 (used 6 x 8)
7 (one fact off); 42 (subtracted instead of dividing)
8 (one fact off); 32 (subtracted)
6 (one fact off); 54 (subtracted)
17 (added); 50 (used 5 x 10)
7 (one fact off); 49 (subtracted)

redirect_script.prompt: 7 x 6 means 7 groups of 6. Start from a fact you own: if 7 x 5 is 35, one more group of 7 makes 42. Say the whole fact out loud.
redirect_script.praise: You built the fact from one you already knew, that is how fluency grows.

vocabulary.definition: The answer you get when you multiply two numbers.
A number being multiplied. In 7 x 6, both 7 and 6 are factors.
The answer you get when you divide one number by another.

next_steps.if_fail: Practice one fact family a day with arrays and flash cards before returning to this skill.

worked_example_script.text: Picture 7 rows with 6 dots in each row. If someone answers 7 + 6 = 13, is 13 dots anywhere near 7 full rows? Even 7 rows of 5 would be 35, so about how big should the real answer be?
Write on the board: 7 x 6 = ?
What does 7 x 6 mean: how many groups, and how many in each group?
Is there a nearby fact you already own, like 7 x 5? What is it?
7 x 5 is 35, so 7 x 6 is just one more group of 7. 35 and 7 more is 42.
If the student says 13, they added. Draw 7 rows of 6 dots and have them count. The picture does the arguing.
Now write: 42 / 6 = ?
Division undoes multiplication. If 7 x 6 = 42, then 42 divided by 6 must be what?
7. Every multiplication fact you own gives you two division facts for free.

skills.name: Break apart multiplication with an area model

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply by breaking a factor into a sum and adding the partial products, shown with an array or area model.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: How can you use 7 x 5 and 7 x 2 to find 7 x 7?

skills.i_do_script: 6 x 7 can be split into friendly pieces. Picture a rectangle 6 rows tall and 7 wide: that is 6 x 7 squares. If I slide a line to cut the 7 into 5 and 2, I get a 6 by 5 block and a 6 by 2 block. 6 x 5 is 30 and 6 x 2 is 12, and 30 + 12 is 42, the same as 6 x 7. Breaking a factor into parts and adding the pieces is exactly the move you will use later to expand 6(x + 2), so we build it here with plain numbers first.

canonical_error.pattern: After breaking a factor, multiplies only one part and forgets the other partial product
canonical_error.example: For 6 x (5 + 2), writes 6 x 5 = 30 and stops, missing 6 x 2 = 12, so answers 30 instead of 42
canonical_error.why: The student splits the factor but counts only the first piece, so the second block of rows is never added. On the area model half the rectangle is left uncounted. This is the same slip that later drops the second term when distributing 6(x + 2).

skills.item_template: A product found by breaking one factor into a sum and adding the partial products, whole numbers within the tables. NR response, no calculator. Short stems for a fluency sprint.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 30 (kept only 6 x 5); 32 (added the partial products wrong)
12 (kept only 4 x 3); 20 (kept only 4 x 5)

sample_items.stem: Use 7 x 5 = 35 and 7 x 3 = 21 to find 7 x 8.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 35 (stopped at the first partial product); 21 (kept only the second)
18 (kept only 3 x 6); 12 (kept only 3 x 4)

sample_items.stem: Break 8 into 5 + 3 to find 6 x 8: 6 x 5 + 6 x 3 = ?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 30 (kept only 6 x 5); 18 (kept only 6 x 3)
20 (kept only one 5 x 4); 24 (added the parts wrong)

sample_items.stem: Use 9 x 5 = 45 and 9 x 2 = 18 to find 9 x 7.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 45 (stopped at the first partial product); 18 (kept only the second)
20 (kept only 2 x 10); 23 (added 10 + 3 then the extra 2 x 3 wrong)

redirect_script.stop: Did you count BOTH parts of the rectangle?
redirect_script.prompt: Breaking a factor makes two blocks, so it makes two products. Find both partial products, then add them for the total.
redirect_script.praise: Both blocks counted, both products added, that is the whole total.

vocabulary.definition: A number being multiplied.
The product of one part after you break a factor apart, like 6 x 5 in 6 x (5 + 2).
A rectangle whose side lengths are the factors. Its area is the product.

next_steps.if_fail: Practice building single products as arrays and area models before breaking factors apart.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a rectangle 6 rows tall and 7 squares wide. Draw one vertical line to split the 7 into 5 and 2.
The left block is 6 rows of 5. How many squares is that? The right block is 6 rows of 2. How many is that?
30 squares and 12 squares. Put them together: 30 + 12 = 42, which is 6 x 7. Breaking the 7 into 5 + 2 did not change the total, it just made two easier products.
If a student counts only the left block and says 30, point at the right block: these rows are still 6 tall. Have they been counted?
Your turn: split the 8 into 5 + 3 to find 6 x 8. What are the two partial products, and what is their sum?

skills.name: Evaluate numerical expressions using order of operations

prerequisite_skill.description: Evaluate a numerical expression by doing grouping symbols first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

skills.i_do_script: A numerical expression can have several operations, and they do not just run left to right. There is an order: do anything inside grouping symbols first, then multiply and divide, and only then add and subtract. Watch 2 + 3 x 4. The multiplication goes first: 3 x 4 is 12, then 2 + 12 is 14, not 20. And in 3 x (4 + 5), the parentheses go first: 4 + 5 is 9, then 3 x 9 is 27. The order is a traffic rule that keeps everyone getting the same answer.

canonical_error.pattern: Works strictly left to right, ignoring that grouping and multiplication or division come first
canonical_error.example: Computes 2 + 3 x 4 as 5 x 4 = 20 instead of 2 + 12 = 14
canonical_error.why: The student reads the expression like a sentence, left to right, and performs each operation as it appears. Multiplication and division outrank addition and subtraction, so 3 x 4 must happen before the 2 is added.

skills.item_template: A numerical expression with two or three operations, sometimes with parentheses, whole numbers only. Student evaluates to a single number. NR response, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Which is the value of 2 + 3 x 4?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 20 works left to right, adding 2 + 3 before multiplying; 24 multiplies all three as 2 x 3 x 4; 9 adds every number as 2 + 3 + 4

redirect_script.stop: Which operation has to happen first here?
redirect_script.prompt: Grouping symbols first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. Circle the multiplication or the parentheses and do that step before the addition.
redirect_script.praise: You followed the order instead of going left to right, that is what keeps the answer honest.

vocabulary.definition: The agreed order for evaluating: grouping symbols, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
Parentheses or brackets that mark a part to evaluate first.
Do the operations to find the single number an expression equals.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 2 + 3 x 4
Two operations here. Which one outranks the other, add or multiply?
Multiply first. 3 x 4 is 12, and now the expression is 2 + 12.
Finish it: 2 + 12 is what?
If a student adds 2 + 3 first and gets 20, ask which operation the order rule says goes first. Multiply before add.
Now write: 3 x (4 + 5)
What changes when there are parentheses? What do we do first now?
Parentheses first: 4 + 5 is 9, then 3 x 9 is 27.
Your turn: evaluate 20 - 6 x 2. Name the first step out loud.

practice_problems.stem: Sam evaluated an expression. Find the mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Sam added before multiplying. The order rule says multiply first: 3 x 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

activities.title: Build the Group First
activities.instructions:
1. Give each pair the expression 3 x (4 + 5) and a pile of counters.
2. Build the parentheses first: make one group of 4 and one group of 5 and push them together to see 9.
3. Now make 3 copies of that group of 9 and count the total, 27.
4. Compare with a partner who ignored the parentheses and did 3 x 4 then added 5. Which count matches the rule?
5. Repeat with 2 x (6 + 1). Say each time: build the grouped part first, then do the rest.

activities.title: Order Race
activities.instructions:
1. Deal each group a stack of expression cards like 20 - 6 x 2.
2. On go, each player evaluates the top card on a whiteboard, naming the first step out loud.
3. Players check each other: a left-to-right answer loses the card.
4. Cards with parentheses are worth two points because the grouping step is the easy one to skip.
5. First to eight points wins. Debrief: which card tempted you to go left to right?

strategy_links.why: Building the parenthesized group with counters before combining it makes 'do the grouping first' physical before the order rule is named.
Naming each step aloud, multiply before add, models the decision the left-to-right error skips.
The 2 + 3 x 4 = 20 slip is a stable, clean find-and-fix target.

questioning_prompts: Two operations are here. Which one does the order rule do first?
Is there anything inside grouping symbols? Then that goes before everything else.
Why does 2 + 3 x 4 not equal 20?
After you multiply, read the expression again. What is left to do?
How would a calculator that only went left to right get this wrong?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student evaluates left to right, getting 20 for 2 + 3 x 4.
misconception_redirects.say: Multiplication outranks addition. Do 3 x 4 first, then add the 2. Circle the multiplication before you touch the plus sign.
misconception_redirects.praise: You did the higher ranked operation first, that is the whole rule.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student does the parentheses but then still goes left to right outside them.
misconception_redirects.say: Parentheses first was right. Now among what is left, multiply and divide before you add or subtract.
misconception_redirects.praise: Grouping first, then multiply before add, exactly the order.

quick_checks.prompt: Evaluate 4 + 6 x 3 and tell me your first step.
quick_checks.look_for: 22, with 'multiply 6 x 3 first.' An answer of 30 means left to right, adding 4 + 6 first. Rerun the order rule.
3, doing the parentheses before dividing. Dividing 18 by 4 first signals the grouping step was skipped.

steps.annotation: Two operations. Multiplication outranks addition, so it goes first.
Do the multiplication before touching the plus sign.
Now add. The value is 14, not the 20 you get by going left to right.
Grouping symbols first: finish the parentheses.
Multiply before you add.
Add the last two numbers.
State the value.

sentence_starters: The first step is ___ because grouping and multiplication come before ___.
I did not go left to right; I did ___ before ___.

skills.name: Write and interpret numerical expressions with grouping symbols

prerequisite_skill.description: Write a numerical expression that records a described calculation using grouping symbols, and interpret an expression without evaluating it.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Write an expression for: add 6 and 4, then multiply the sum by 3.

skills.i_do_script: An expression can record a set of directions in symbols, and the order of the words tells me where the grouping goes. Take add 6 and 4, then multiply the sum by 3. The adding happens first and to one whole sum, so I wrap it: (6 + 4), then multiply by 3, giving 3 x (6 + 4). Without doing any arithmetic I can also read an expression: 3 x (6 + 4) says take the sum of 6 and 4 and make it three times as big. Reading and writing this structure is the same thinking you will use when 6(x + 2) means six times the whole quantity x + 2.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops the grouping symbols, writing the operations in the order the words appear
canonical_error.example: For add 6 and 4, then multiply by 3, writes 6 + 4 x 3, which multiplies only the 4 and gives 18 instead of 30
canonical_error.why: The student translates word by word and never marks that the whole sum, not just the last number, gets multiplied. Without the parentheses the order rule multiplies 4 by 3 first, so the 6 is left out of the multiplication.

skills.item_template: A described calculation to translate into an expression with grouping symbols, or an expression to interpret in words or compare in size without computing. Whole numbers. Short NR or MC response.

sample_items.stem: Write an expression: add 5 and 3, then multiply the sum by 4.
Write an expression: multiply 6 by 7, then add 2.
Without computing, which is larger: 3 x (20 + 4) or (20 + 4)?
sample_items.answer: 3 x (20 + 4), it is three times as large

sample_items.stem: Write an expression: subtract 3 from 10, then multiply the result by 2.
What does 5 x (8 + 2) tell you to do first, and then what?
sample_items.answer: Add 8 and 2 first, then multiply the sum by 5

sample_items.stem: Write an expression: add 12 and 8, then divide the sum by 5.
Which expression means multiply the sum of 6 and 4 by 3?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 6 + 4 x 3 drops the grouping and multiplies only the 4; 3 x 6 + 4 multiplies only the 6; 6 + 4 + 3 adds everything

sample_items.stem: Without computing, is 2 x (45 + 9) more than, less than, or equal to 45 + 9?
sample_items.answer: More than, it is twice as large

redirect_script.stop: Does the whole sum get multiplied, or just one number?
redirect_script.prompt: If the words say add first, wrap that sum in parentheses before you multiply. Then the multiplier acts on the whole group, not just the last number.
redirect_script.praise: You grouped the sum first, so the multiply lands on the whole thing.

vocabulary.definition: A combination of numbers and operations that names a value, like 3 x (6 + 4).
Parentheses that hold a part together so it is treated as one amount.
The result of adding, and the whole amount inside the parentheses here.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: add 8 and 7, then multiply the sum by 2.
Which operation happens first, and to how much of the expression?
Adding is first, and it makes one sum, 8 + 7. Wrap it in parentheses so it stays together: (8 + 7).
Now write 2 x (8 + 7).
Why can I not just write 2 x 8 + 7?
Without the parentheses only the 8 gets doubled and the 7 is left out. The parentheses keep the whole sum together for the doubling.
If a student writes 8 + 7 x 2, ask them to point to what got multiplied. Just the 7, not the whole sum they were told to double.
Your turn: write an expression for subtract 4 from 10, then multiply the result by 3.

practice_problems.stem: Write an expression: add 3 and 5, then multiply the sum by 2.
In 4 x (6 + 1), what do you do first?
Write an expression: multiply 7 by 3, then add 4.
Without computing, which is larger: 6 x (10 + 2) or (10 + 2)?
practice_problems.answer: 6 x (10 + 2), it is six times as large

practice_problems.stem: Write an expression: subtract 2 from 9, then multiply the result by 5.
What does 3 x (8 + 4) tell you to do first, and then what?
practice_problems.answer: Add 8 and 4 first, then multiply the sum by 3

practice_problems.stem: Write two different expressions that both mean twice the sum of 6 and 4.
Mia wrote an expression for add 6 and 4, then multiply the sum by 3. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: add 6 and 4, then multiply the sum by 3
practice_problems.answer: 6 + 4 x 3 multiplies only the 4 and equals 18. The whole sum must be multiplied, so wrap it: 3 x (6 + 4), which is 30.

activities.title: Say It, Build It, Write It
activities.instructions:
1. One partner reads a direction card like add 5 and 3, then multiply the sum by 4.
2. The other builds it with counters: first make the sum 5 + 3 as one group of 8, then make 4 copies of that group.
3. Together they write the matching expression with parentheses: 4 x (5 + 3).
4. Swap roles with subtract 2 from 9, then double it.
5. Say each time: the words that come first go inside the parentheses.

activities.title: Match the Meaning
materials: Card deck: word-phrase cards and expression cards, two decoys
activities.instructions:
1. Spread word-phrase cards and expression cards face up, including two decoy expressions that drop the parentheses.
2. Players match each phrase to its correct expression, saying which part is the grouped sum.
3. To claim a match, the player states what would go wrong if the parentheses were removed.
4. Set the two decoys aside and rewrite them correctly.
5. Debrief: how do the parentheses change what gets multiplied?

strategy_links.why: Building the grouped sum with counters before making copies makes the parentheses stand for 'do this part first' before the symbols are written.
Partners must agree which operation happens first and defend the grouping before writing, which surfaces the dropped parentheses error.
Writing 6 + 4 x 3 for add then multiply is the stable error; finding and fixing it confronts it directly.

questioning_prompts: Which operation do the words tell you to do first?
Does the whole sum get multiplied, or just the last number?
Where do the parentheses go, and why there?
Read 3 x (6 + 4) back to me in words without computing it.
How would the value change if you erased the parentheses?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes 6 + 4 x 3 for add 6 and 4 then multiply by 3.
misconception_redirects.say: Point to what gets multiplied in what you wrote. Only the 4. The words said multiply the whole sum, so wrap 6 + 4 in parentheses first.
misconception_redirects.praise: The parentheses keep the whole sum together for the multiply.

misconception_redirects.say: The parentheses hold the 6 and 4 together as one amount. Add them first, to 10, then take three of that.
misconception_redirects.praise: You treated the group as one amount, that is what the parentheses mean.

quick_checks.prompt: Write an expression for add 7 and 2, then multiply the sum by 5.
quick_checks.look_for: 5 x (7 + 2). Writing 7 + 2 x 5 drops the grouping and multiplies only the 2. Rerun the wrap-the-sum step.

quick_checks.prompt: Without computing, is 4 x (10 + 5) bigger or smaller than 10 + 5?
quick_checks.look_for: Bigger, four times as large. A student who has to compute has not yet read the structure.

worked_solution.stem: Write an expression for: add 8 and 7, then multiply the sum by 2.

steps.annotation: The words say add before multiply, and it makes one sum.
Wrap the sum in parentheses so it stays together.
Multiply the whole grouped sum by 2. Not 2 x 8 + 7, which would leave the 7 out.

faded_example.stem: Write an expression for: subtract 4 from 10, then multiply the result by 3.

steps.annotation: The words say subtract before multiply, and it makes one result.
Wrap the difference in parentheses so the whole result stays together.
Multiply the grouped result by 3.
Write the finished expression.

sentence_starters: The words say ___ first, so I wrap ___ in parentheses.
The 3 multiplies the whole ___, not just the ___.

skills.name: Identify variables, coefficients, constants, and terms in expressions
skills.i_do_script: Picture 7x + 4 as stuff on a table: 7 identical mystery boxes, each holding x marbles, plus 4 loose marbles beside them. The 7 counts boxes of x; the 4 just sits there no matter what. Those two very different jobs are about to get names. Every algebra expression is built from parts with names, and today we learn the names. Look at 5x + 8. It has two terms, separated by the plus sign: 5x and 8. In the term 5x, the letter x is the variable and the 5 riding in front of it is the coefficient -- the number multiplying the variable. The 8 has no variable at all, so it's the constant. I'm going to point at parts and you'll name them, like labeling the parts of a bike.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses the coefficient with the constant -- names whichever number is most visible
canonical_error.example: For 6m + 5, student says the coefficient of m is 5 because 5 is 'the other number'
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'coefficient' and 'constant' as interchangeable words for 'a number in the expression.' They haven't anchored coefficient to its job: the number MULTIPLYING the variable, physically attached to it.

redirect_script.stop: Which number is actually touching the variable?
redirect_script.prompt: Picture the boxes: is that number counting boxes of x, or is it loose marbles on the table? Circle the term that contains the variable. The coefficient lives INSIDE that circle, glued to the letter. The constant is the loner term with no letter at all. Now which is which?
redirect_script.praise: You anchored each name to its job -- coefficient multiplies, constant stands alone.

skills.item_template: An expression like 7x + 4 is given. Student identifies the coefficient of the variable, the constant term, or the number of terms. MC with 4 choices.

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

  7x + 4

What is the coefficient of x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 is the constant mistaken for the coefficient; 11 adds the two numbers; x confuses variable with coefficient

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

  3n + 9

What is the constant term?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 is the coefficient mistaken for the constant; 12 adds the numbers; n confuses variable with constant

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

  5y + 2 + 3y

How many terms are in this expression?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 counts only the y-terms; 1 treats the whole expression as one thing; 10 adds the visible numbers

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

  m + 6

What is the coefficient of m?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0 assumes no visible number means zero; 6 grabs the constant; m confuses variable with coefficient

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

  4a + 7b + 2

What is the coefficient of b?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 grabs the first coefficient seen; 2 grabs the constant; b confuses variable with coefficient

vocabulary.definition: The letter that stands for a number, like the x in 5x + 8.
The number multiplying the variable -- the 5 in 5x.
A term that is just a number with no variable -- the 8 in 5x + 8.
A single piece of the expression, separated from the others by + signs.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the expression as objects: 7x + 4 is 7 identical mystery boxes (each hiding x marbles) plus 4 loose marbles sitting on the table.

Suppose each box turns out to hold 10 marbles -- how many marbles in all? (7 x 10 + 4 = 74.) Now suppose each box holds only 2 -- how many? (7 x 2 + 4 = 18.) Which number's contribution changed with x, the 7 or the 4?

The 7 rides with the boxes -- it multiplies whatever x turns out to be -- while the 4 stays 4 no matter what. Glued-to-the-boxes versus sitting-alone is the entire difference between the two numbers, and each job gets its own name.
Write on the board: 7x + 4
How many pieces do you see in 7x + 4, and what symbol separates them?
Right -- the plus sign splits it into two terms: 7x and 4. Draw a box around each term.
Look inside the first box, 7x. Which symbol is the variable, and what is the 7 doing to it?
The 7 is multiplying the x -- that's why we call it the coefficient. Coefficient means 'the multiplier glued to the letter.'
Now look at the second box, 4. Does it have a variable? So what do we call a term that's just a number sitting alone?

If the student names 4 as the coefficient of x, they grabbed the loner number. Ask: 'Is the 4 touching the x? Circle the term with the variable -- the coefficient lives inside that circle. So which number multiplies x?'
So in 7x + 4 the coefficient of x is 7, and the 4 is the constant. Coefficient multiplies the variable; the constant stands alone.

practice_problems.stem: In the expression 8x + 3, what is the coefficient of x?
In the expression 2y + 7, what is the constant term?
How many terms are in the expression 4n + 9 + 2n?
practice_problems.notes: Watch for students who count only the n-terms and say 2.

practice_problems.stem: In the expression x + 12, what is the coefficient of x?
practice_problems.notes: The invisible 1 -- expect '0' or '12.'

practice_problems.stem: Jayden labeled the parts of an expression. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Jayden says: the coefficient of m is 5,
because 5 is the other number in the expression.
practice_problems.answer: The coefficient of m is 6 -- the number multiplying (touching) the variable. The 5 is the constant, the term with no variable.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical coefficient/constant swap, as an item.

practice_problems.stem: In the expression 3a + 4b + 2, name BOTH coefficients.
Write an expression with a coefficient of 5, a variable y, and a constant of 2.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- producing from the vocabulary instead of naming.

practice_problems.stem: In the expression 2x + x + 8, what is the coefficient of the SECOND x term? Explain how you know.
practice_problems.answer: 1 -- x alone means 1x; the coefficient 1 is invisible but still there.
practice_problems.notes: Combines the invisible-1 idea with careful term-by-term reading.

activities.title: Name That Part
activities.instructions:
1. Write the expression 7k + 3 + 2m at the top of the table where both partners can see it.
2. Spread the 12 cards face up. Each card names a piece pulled from that expression or a claim about it.
3. Partners sort every card under Variable, Coefficient, Constant, or Whole Term.
4. For each card, the placer must finish the sentence: 'It's a ___ because its job is ___.'
5. Debrief question: which card was hardest to place, and what job finally decided it?

cards.text: the number 3, standing alone with no variable
the 1 hiding in front of a lone x

activities.title: Whiteboard Part Hunt
activities.instructions:
1. Write an expression on the board, e.g. 9y + 4 + 3y.
2. Call out a part name: 'coefficient of the first y-term!' Students write just that number and flash their boards.
3. Anyone who writes the constant when you asked for a coefficient explains the difference to the group -- teaching it back earns the point.
4. Escalate to traps: 'coefficient of x in x + 5' (answer: 1) and 'the constant in 4n' (answer: there isn't one).
5. Debrief: which part name fooled the most boards, and why?

strategy_links.why: Part names (coefficient, constant, term) are pure vocabulary automaticity -- choral response drills the name-to-job link fast.
Whiteboard Pass shows instantly which students are swapping coefficient and constant.
The coefficient/constant swap is a clean find-and-fix target for error analysis.

questioning_prompts: Which number is physically touching the variable? What does touching mean it's doing?

skills.name: Combine like terms to write equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: Like terms are terms that count the same thing. In 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r, the r-terms count r's and the plain numbers count ones -- so they live in separate piles. Watch me sort: 6r + r + 2r is 9r (remember, r alone is 1r), and 6 + 2 is 8. The whole thing becomes 9r + 8. Same value, shorter name. The one rule: r's only combine with r's, and numbers only combine with numbers.

canonical_error.pattern: Merges unlike terms -- adds constants into coefficients as if every number were the same kind
canonical_error.example: Simplifies 4x + 5 + 2x as 11x, adding the 4, 5, and 2 together
canonical_error.why: The student sees three numbers and adds them all, ignoring what each number counts. 4x counts x's and 5 counts ones -- different units, like adding 4 dogs + 5 cats and calling it 11 dogs.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- do all of those terms count the same thing?
redirect_script.prompt: Underline every term that has the variable, and circle every plain number. Only the underlined ones can combine with each other, and only the circled ones can combine with each other. Now re-add each pile.
redirect_script.praise: You sorted before you added -- that's exactly what combining like terms means.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r

So 6r + 6 + r + 2 + 2r = 9r + 8. Same value for any r -- we just gave it a shorter name. That's what 'equivalent expressions' means.

skills.name: Apply commutative and associative properties to write equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: When we combined like terms, we quietly rearranged the expression first -- and today we name the rules that make that legal. The commutative property says order doesn't matter for addition: 9 + 6n and 6n + 9 name the same number. The associative property says grouping doesn't matter for addition: (4y + 6y) + y and 4y + (6y + y) are the same. But here's the catch -- these rules are ONLY for addition and multiplication. 15 - b is NOT the same as b - 15, and we can prove it by plugging in a number.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the commutative property to subtraction or division -- believes 'order never matters'
canonical_error.example: Student claims 15 - b is equivalent to b - 15 'by the commutative property'
canonical_error.why: The student learned 'you can switch the order' as a universal rule instead of a property OF addition and multiplication. They've never tested it on subtraction, where b = 5 gives 15 - 5 = 10 but 5 - 15 does not.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- does switching work for THAT operation?
redirect_script.prompt: Test it with a real number. Let the variable be 5: work out both orders and compare. If the two answers differ, the commutative property doesn't cover that operation -- it only covers addition and multiplication.
redirect_script.praise: You tested instead of assuming -- that's how mathematicians check a property's limits.

skills.item_template: An expression is given. Student selects or writes an equivalent expression formed by the commutative property (reorder) or associative property (regroup), or names the property used. MC or short NR. Rearrangements use addition only, per content limits.

vocabulary.definition: For addition and multiplication, the order can switch without changing the value: a + b = b + a.
For addition and multiplication, the grouping (parentheses) can move without changing the value: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
Adding 0 or multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged: k + 0 = k and 1 x k = k.
Two expressions that name the same number for every value of the variable.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 9 + 6n     6n + 9
Do these two expressions name the same number? How could we find out without just trusting our eyes?
Let n = 2. What does each expression equal?
Both are 21. Switching the order of an ADDITION never changes the value -- that's the commutative property. 'Commute' means to move back and forth, like commuting to school.
Now write: 15 - b     b - 15
A student says these are equivalent by the commutative property. Let b = 5 -- what does each side give you?

Students should get 10 for 15 - 5 and see that 5 - 15 can't also be 10. If someone insists they're equal, have them act it out: having 15 dollars and spending 5 is not the same as having 5 and spending 15.
So the commutative property has a boundary: addition and multiplication only. Never subtraction, never division. When in doubt, test a value -- the numbers always tell the truth.

practice_problems.stem: Use the commutative property to rewrite n + 12.

practice_problems.answer: True -- the commutative property of addition.

practice_problems.stem: Which is equivalent to 8 + 3x: 3x + 8 or 8x + 3? Explain your choice.
practice_problems.answer: 3x + 8 -- the commutative property moves whole TERMS. 8x + 3 swaps the numbers' jobs and changes the value (try x = 2: 14 vs 19).
practice_problems.notes: The terms-move-whole idea; expect students to pick 8x + 3 by pattern-matching digits.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus used a property to rewrite an expression. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Not equivalent. Test b = 5: 15 - 5 = 10, but 5 - 15 does not equal 10. The commutative property covers ONLY addition and multiplication -- subtraction has no such property.
practice_problems.notes: The commutative-works-for-subtraction trap, head on.

practice_problems.stem: Rewrite 4y + (6y + y) + 17 with the parentheses regrouped, using the associative property.
practice_problems.answer: (4y + 6y) + y + 17 (answers may vary; any regrouping of the added terms is correct)

practice_problems.stem: Name the property: (2 + 9) + n = 2 + (9 + n).
Write TWO different expressions equivalent to 7 + 5k + 3 using the commutative or associative properties.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own; the regrouped (7 + 3) + 5k sets up combining to 5k + 10.

practice_problems.stem: Ava says 20 / m = m / 20 by the commutative property. Test m = 4 and explain what her test shows.
practice_problems.answer: Not equivalent: 20 / 4 = 5 but 4 / 20 = 0.2. Division, like subtraction, is not commutative -- one counterexample is enough to sink the claim.
practice_problems.notes: Extends the boundary from subtraction to division.

printable_artifact.instructions: Each property is a legal move for rewriting an expression. The two on the bottom row are the traps -- they are NOT legal moves.

skills.name: Apply the distributive property to expand and factor expressions
skills.i_do_script: The distributive property lets multiplication reach across a sum. 3(2x + 5) means 3 groups of (2x + 5) -- so I get 3 groups of 2x AND 3 groups of 5. Watch: 3 x 2x is 6x, and 3 x 5 is 15, so 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15. The 3 must visit BOTH terms inside the parentheses -- that's the whole property. And it runs backwards too: given 12x + 8, I find the greatest common factor 4 and pull it out: 4(3x + 2).

canonical_error.pattern: Partial distribution -- multiplies only the first term inside the parentheses
canonical_error.why: The student treats the multiplier as touching only the term it's physically next to. They see 4(3x...) and multiply, then copy the + 5 down unchanged -- the 4 never 'visits' the second term. An area model or a test value exposes the missing 4 x 5.

redirect_script.stop: Did your multiplier visit BOTH terms?

redirect_script.praise: Both arrows, both products -- that's the distributive property done right.

vocabulary.definition: A multiplier outside parentheses multiplies EVERY term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Use the distributive property to remove the parentheses: 3(2x + 5) becomes 6x + 15.

The largest number that divides evenly into both terms.
What lives inside the parentheses -- two terms joined by a plus sign, like 2x + 5.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 3(2x + 5). Below it, draw a rectangle with height 3, split into two sections labeled 2x and 5 along the top.
3(2x + 5) means 3 groups of (2x + 5). If this rectangle is 3 tall and (2x + 5) long, what is the area of the LEFT section?
And the area of the RIGHT section -- 3 rows of 5 is what?
So the total area is 6x + 15. The 3 multiplied BOTH sections -- it had to, because both sections are 3 tall.
Draw two arrows from the 3: one to 2x, one to 5. Write: 3 x 2x = 6x and 3 x 5 = 15.
If a student writes 6x + 5, point at the right section of the rectangle: 'This part is 3 tall too. Is its area just 5?' The picture catches the missing multiplication better than words.
Now let's check with a number. Let x = 1. What is 3(2 + 5)? What is 6 + 15? What would the wrong answer 6 + 5 give?
Your turn, backwards: 12x + 8. What's the biggest number that divides both 12 and 8? Pull it out and write the factored form.

skills.name: Justify whether two expressions are equivalent using substitution
skills.i_do_script: Two expressions are equivalent when they name the same number no matter what value the variable takes. So substitution is our lie detector. A student claims 3.5(x + 6) equals 3.5x + 21. Let's test x = 2: the left side is 3.5 times 8, which is 28, and the right side is 7 plus 21, which is 28. Same number -- the claim survives. But if even ONE value gives two different numbers, the expressions are not equivalent, case closed. Looks can lie; substitution can't.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges equivalence by appearance -- 'same numbers and letters' -- instead of testing a value
canonical_error.example: Claims 2(x + 3) and 2x + 3 are equivalent 'because both have a 2, an x, and a 3'
canonical_error.why: The student thinks equivalent means 'made of the same ingredients' rather than 'names the same number for every value.' They've never operationalized the definition, so a near-miss like 2x + 3 looks identical to the real expansion 2x + 6.

redirect_script.stop: Don't trust your eyes -- run the test.
redirect_script.prompt: Pick a value like x = 4 and substitute it into BOTH expressions separately. Work each one all the way to a single number. Do the two numbers match?
redirect_script.praise: You let the numbers decide instead of the way it looks -- that's a real justification.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'A student says 3.5(x + 6) = 3.5x + 21. Use x = 2 to decide if the student is correct.'
Before any math: what does 'equivalent' actually promise? Equal for which values?
Equal for EVERY value. So we test one and see if the claim survives. Substitution is our lie detector.
Left side: 3.5(2 + 6) = 3.5 x 8 = 28. Write each step.
Now you do the right side: 3.5 x 2 + 21. Work it all the way to one number.
Watch that students evaluate 3.5 x 2 as 7 before adding 21 -- multiply before add. If someone adds 2 + 21 first, ask which operation goes first.
28 and 28. What's our verdict -- and how would the verdict change if we'd gotten 28 and 25?
One mismatch would sink the claim forever -- that's a counterexample. Matching values support the claim, and the distributive property tells us it holds for every x, not just 2.

so they are the same expression.
practice_problems.answer: Leo never substituted a value. Test x = 2: 3(2 + 4) = 18 but 3(2) + 4 = 10. Not equivalent -- 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Same ingredients does not mean same value.
practice_problems.notes: The judging-by-appearance error -- the fix is running the test.

practice_problems.answer: Not equivalent. At x = 3: 2(3) + 4 = 10 but 6(3) = 18. One matching value was a coincidence -- equivalence must hold for every value.

activities.title: Lie Detector
materials: Claim cards (an equation that may be true or false)

Thinking aloud through 'equivalent means equal for EVERY value, so I'll test one' models the justification structure itself.

skills.name: Combine properties to simplify and write multiple equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: Now we chain the properties together. Take 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1. First the distributive property clears the parentheses: 6x + 8. Now the expression is 6x + 8 + 5x + 1, and the commutative property lets me regroup: 6x + 5x is 11x, and 8 + 1 is 9. Final answer: 11x + 9. The order matters -- distribute FIRST, then combine. The 5x outside the parentheses can't jump inside before the 2 has done its job.

canonical_error.pattern: Pulls outside terms into the parentheses before distributing -- combines across the grouping
canonical_error.why: The student treats the parentheses as decoration, so 4x looks like just another term to gather. But the parentheses mark what the 3 multiplies -- moving 4x inside makes the 3 multiply it too, tripling a term that was never supposed to be tripled.

redirect_script.stop: Freeze -- has the multiplier done its job yet?

redirect_script.praise: Distribute, then combine -- you ran the properties in the right order.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1
There are two jobs here -- distributing and combining like terms. Which has to happen first, and what decides that?
The parentheses are a locked room: the 2 multiplies ONLY what's inside. The 5x and the 1 are outside the room, so they wait.
Distribute the 2 -- both arrows. What does 2(3x + 4) become?
Rewrite the whole expression with no parentheses: 6x + 8 + 5x + 1.
Now which property lets us reorder and regroup these four terms? Gather the piles: what are the x-terms, and what are the constants?
If a student had wanted to write 2(3x + 4 + 5x) at the start, test it now: x = 1 gives the original 2(7) + 5 + 1 = 20, but 2(3 + 4 + 5) = 24. The locked room matters.
6x + 5x is 11x, and 8 + 1 is 9. So 2(3x + 4) + 5x + 1 = 11x + 9. Distribute first, then commute and combine -- three properties, one clean chain.

activities.title: The Locked Room
activities.instructions:

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student gathers an outside term into the parentheses before distributing -- turns 3(2x + 1) + 4x into 3(6x + 1).
misconception_redirects.say: The parentheses are a locked room: only what's inside gets multiplied. Distribute first and write the expression with no parentheses at all. THEN gather your like terms.
misconception_redirects.praise: Distribute, then combine -- you ran the properties in the right order.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student distributes to the first term only in the multi-step setting -- 2(3x + 4) + 5x becomes 6x + 4 + 5x.
misconception_redirects.say: Two terms inside means two arrows -- the 2 owes the 4 a multiplication too. Redo just the distribution step, then bring the 5x back in.
misconception_redirects.praise: Both arrows first, outside terms after -- that's the full chain.

quick_checks.prompt: Simplify 2(n + 3) + 4n, narrating each property as you use it.
quick_checks.look_for: Distributive (2n + 6), then commutative/combining (6n + 6). An answer of 2(5n + 3) = 10n + 6 means the outside 4n got smuggled inside -- rerun the locked-room routine.

quick_checks.prompt: Give me TWO expressions equivalent to 8(2x + 3), each made with a different property.
quick_checks.look_for: E.g. 16x + 24 (distributive) and 8(3 + 2x) (commutative) or 4(4x + 6) (refactoring). Only producing the expansion suggests the student has one tool, not a toolbox.

steps.annotation: The parentheses go first. The 2 multiplies both inside terms -- the 5x and 1 wait outside.
No parentheses left. Now the commutative property lets us gather like terms.
Combine each pile separately -- x's with x's, ones with ones.
Check with x = 1: original is 2(7) + 5 + 1 = 20, and 11(1) + 9 = 20. Equivalent.
Clear the parentheses first -- both arrows. The 3y and 4 wait outside.
Rewrite the whole expression with no parentheses.
Gather the piles: add the y-terms, then add the constants.
Write the simplified expression, then check it with y = 1.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, applying the distributive property, the at-proficiency core of the standard. If the student passes, move up to S5 (justify equivalence by substitution) and S6 (chain properties for multiple equivalent forms). If S4 fails, drop below grade level: B1 checks order of operations with grouping symbols and B2 checks writing and interpreting numerical expressions, the two grade five skills that expression work leans on. If those wobble, the foundations locate the gap in grades 3 to 4: F1 is multiplication and division fact fluency and F2 is the number based distributive property shown with an area model. S1, S2, and S3 stay available to probe the standard's own naming, combining, and rearranging groundwork.
